title: How Does a Botnet Take Over Millions of Devices?
question: How does a botnet take over millions of devices without their owners noticing?
description: This week Google said it had disrupted a hidden network of more than 1.3 million devices, mostly Android TV boxes, that was working for criminals. Learn how a botnet is built, how it makes money through ad fraud and proxy services, and how investigators cut off its control. We explain it step by step with every fact checked. Who should carry more responsibility for stopping this: the companies that certify devices, or the people who buy them?

ad_safety.reason: Educational cybersecurity explainer with no violence, no instructions for attacks, and a neutral tone that attributes claims to Google.

scenes.narration: This week, Google announced it had dismantled a secret network of more than 1.3 million devices, mostly Android TV boxes, that was working for criminals. How does a botnet take over millions of devices?

visual.text: How does a botnet take over millions of devices?

scenes.narration: Owners were never asked for consent. Behind the scenes, the boxes ran hidden jobs such as ad fraud and proxy traffic.

visual.label: A TV box in a living room

scenes.narration: In the next few minutes, you will see how a botnet is built, how it earns money, and how investigators switch it off.
A bot is any connected device that secretly runs software obeying someone else. A botnet is a large group of bots, all taking orders from the same controller.
The controller does not message each device by hand. Every infected device contacts a command-and-control server, often called C2, and waits there for instructions.
A famous example is Mirai, which emerged in 2016. It was used for huge attacks on websites, and its code was later leaked, so other criminals copied it.
Mirai scanned the internet for devices, tried common factory usernames and passwords, and every device that let it in joined the network.
The attacks were simple in idea: thousands of devices request the same website at once, until real visitors cannot get through.
But what if nobody has to break in at all, because the hidden software was installed before the box even reached a shop?

visual.text: What if the device arrives already infected?

scenes.narration: According to Google, that is what happened with XCPE. Firmware is the built-in software a device runs from the moment it switches on, and the manufacturer writes it.

visual.label: Firmware is written at the factory

scenes.narration: Google says the maker, Videostrong Technology, based in Shenzhen, China, built a backdoor called x.cpe into many device models and brands over several years.
The backdoor ran at system level, the same level as the operating system itself. If someone deletes it, reports say it reinstalls itself from another part of the device's own storage.

The backdoor contacts its control servers for instructions. To install software silently, it also switches off the app checks in Google Play Protect, Android's built-in security feature, and wipes the record of user consent.
More than 1.3 million devices were enrolled, mostly Android TV boxes, but also telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signs.
Google does not believe a rogue employee or a simple mistake was behind it. Its assessment is that the operation was deliberate, and run for profit.

TrendAI's own telemetry counted about 1.47 million devices in more than 170 countries, with the most in Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan. The partners' joint press release says more than 200 countries.
Why would a manufacturer do this to its own customers? Google says it assesses, with high confidence, that the reason was money.

visual.text: Why hijack your own customers' devices?

scenes.narration: Google says Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates and then loaded those affiliates' malicious modules onto the infected devices.
Those modules did three main jobs: ad fraud, residential proxy services, and loading still more malware. Each one turned an ordinary gadget into a small piece of criminal infrastructure.
In ad fraud, a hidden program loads webpages and clicks adverts that no human ever sees, so advertisers pay for attention that never existed.
A residential proxy sends someone else's internet traffic out through your home connection, so websites see an ordinary household instead of the real sender.
Google found that a single infected device ran as many as three separate proxy services at once, all without the owner's knowledge.
For owners, the risk is that their home connection carries strangers' traffic, including criminal traffic, and that data on the device could be copied.
You cannot visit a million living rooms. So investigators go after the one thing every bot depends on: the servers that give the orders.

visual.text: How do you stop a botnet in a million homes?

scenes.narration: Google took legal action against the domains and servers that controlled XCPE and delivered its modules, and against the control systems of more than a dozen other malware families.
Those groups also spread their software by other routes, so Google expects the move to cut off access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
Google worked with Japan's National Police Agency and several security companies, including Lumen, Human Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI.
Google also ended its relationship with Videostrong. The company and any future affiliates are barred from making certified Android devices or supplying software to certified manufacturers.
Google says it tightened firmware integrity checks on certified Android TV devices and changed how it reviews manufacturers, to close the testing gap that was used.

Here is the catch. Cutting off the known servers removes the operators' current control channel, but the backdoor is still in the firmware of affected boxes, and operators have rebuilt on new infrastructure before.

visual.label: The code is still on the boxes

scenes.narration: TrendAI says cleanup needs vendor action, platform protection or replacing the device. Synthient advises discarding affected boxes, so owners may need to replace them.

The takedown happened in late October, and Google published its report on 2 November. It warns that the markets for backdoors, ad fraud and residential proxies are resilient and work as an interconnected supply chain.
Different security firms recommend different steps. Google advises buying connected devices only from reputable manufacturers and checking its Android TV partner list.

items.text: Check the Android TV partner list

scenes.narration: Videostrong was itself a certified partner, so certification alone was no guarantee. TrendAI says companies should treat unmanaged devices on staff home networks as part of their exposure, and keep corporate access behind managed devices.

In one breath: a botnet is hijacked devices obeying one server. XCPE was built in at the factory, earned from ad fraud and proxies, and disrupted by taking down its servers. The backdoor remains in the boxes.
Who should carry more responsibility for stopping this: the companies that certify devices, or the people who buy them? Tell us in the comments.

visual.text: Certifiers or buyers: who is more responsible?

short.outro: Watch the full episode to see how a botnet is built, how it earns money, and how it is switched off.

factcheck.summary: Core facts check out against Google's report and its partners' releases: 1.3M devices, Videostrong, the TrendAI figures, the actions Google took, the partner list and the three-proxy claim. Four wording fixes are needed. The main one is that scene 13 misdescribes the Play Protect/consent mechanism. The others are scene 12 (OS-level overstatement), scene 32 (timing and 'resilient') and scene 6/8 (Mirai scale and targets).

open_issues.claim: it also switches off the app checks in Google Play Protect... and wipes the record of user consent.
open_issues.problem: Google's technical write-up, as relayed by several outlets, says the backdoor sets the package_verifier_user_consent setting to -1. That turns off Play Protect's app verification. Only one secondary summary describes this as wiping consent records. As written, it implies user consent records are erased, which the primary report does not clearly say.
open_issues.fix: To install software silently, it also switches off Google Play Protect's app verification by overwriting a package-verification consent setting.

open_issues.claim: The backdoor ran at system level, the same level as the operating system itself.
open_issues.problem: Sources say x.cpe is a preloaded system app that runs with Android system privileges (android.uid.system). That is not the same as being part of the operating system or kernel. The phrasing overstates it.
open_issues.fix: The backdoor was preloaded as a system app with system-level privileges, so ordinary users cannot uninstall it.

open_issues.claim: The takedown happened in late October... It warns that the markets for backdoors, ad fraud and residential proxies are resilient and work as an interconnected supply chain.
open_issues.problem: Google's own wording is that the takedown happened 'last week' (before the 2 November report). 'Late October' is a reasonable inference that some outlets repeat, but it is not Google's wording. Google describes the ecosystem as an interconnected supply chain and says lasting disruption needs continued effort. I found no source that uses the word 'resilient' for the markets.
open_issues.fix: Google says the takedown happened last week and published its report on 2 November. It warns that backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings and residential proxy providers work as an interconnected supply chain, and that lasting disruption needs continued effort.

open_issues.claim: It was used for huge attacks on websites... (Scene 8) thousands of devices request the same website at once
open_issues.problem: Mirai's best-known 2016 targets were the Krebs on Security site, the French host OVH and the DNS provider Dyn, which disrupted many sites indirectly. Mirai also involved hundreds of thousands of devices, not 'thousands'. This is simplified and understated rather than wrong.
open_issues.fix: It was used for record-breaking attacks in 2016, including on the Dyn DNS provider, which took many popular sites offline. Its code was leaked on 30 September 2016, and others copied it. Attacks use very large numbers of devices at once.
